text: Knowing what chaos engineering tests for is only half of it — running an experiment safely is its own discipline, and skipping it is how a useful practice turns into a self-inflicted outage. This lesson covers the four things that have to be true before any real failure gets injected.

In order: first, pick the smallest blast radius that still teaches you something — one pod, not a whole deployment; one percent of traffic, not all of it. Second, define an abort criterion, a specific measurable threshold that means stop. Third, have an actual kill switch ready to act on that threshold immediately. Fourth, run it during business hours, with the owning team watching dashboards and other teams aware a drill is happening.

Here's what a real abort criterion looks like, written down in advance: if checkout success rate drops below 97 percent for more than 60 seconds, abort immediately. That's deliberately unambiguous. "We'll watch the dashboards and use our judgment" is not a kill switch — by the time judgment kicks in during a live degradation, you're often arguing about whether it's bad enough to stop while it keeps getting worse.

You don't need custom scripts to inject failure this precisely — real tools exist for it. Gremlin is a commercial platform that lets a team dial in specific attacks like latency or CPU exhaustion against a scoped target. Chaos Mesh, a CNCF project for Kubernetes, works declaratively: you define a PodChaos resource, and mode: one tells it to kill exactly one matching pod, not every pod with that label. Neither tool replaces the discipline — they just make it easy to execute precisely and stop.

Put all of that together and a chaos experiment during business hours, watched by the team, with a pre-agreed abort line and a working kill switch, is safer than it sounds — and a surprise overnight test with no one watching is the opposite of rigor. Next lesson scales this idea up from a single technical experiment to a full game day, where the human response process gets tested right alongside the system.
